A *garden-path sentence* leads the reader into one reading
and then forces them back to the start
when the rest of the sentence does not fit
([Wikipedia: Garden-path sentence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden-path_sentence)).
The sentence may be grammatical,
but the reader parses it twice.

Two habits cause most garden paths in technical writing:

- dropping a relative pronoun,
  so that a noun and the subject of the next clause run together
  (see [Do not omit relative pronouns](#do-not-omit-relative-pronouns));
- stacking a noun, a clause and a verb
  so that the reader cannot tell which noun the verb belongs to.

When you reread a sentence and stumble,
restore the missing pronoun,
or reorder the sentence so that each verb follows its subject directly.

::: {#exm-garden-path}

## Rewriting a garden-path sentence

> ❌ Report only SHAs a command you ran printed in full.
>
> ✅ Report only SHAs that were printed in full by a command you ran.

In the first version,
"SHAs a command you ran" reads at first as a single noun phrase,
and "printed" then arrives with no clear subject.
The rewrite adds "that were",
so the reader knows a describing clause has begun,
and puts the verb "printed" next to the noun it describes.

:::
